After their free upgrade during the hurricane, I was reading people's comments on Tesla using software to limit the range of their vehicles and selling an upgrade to unlock the whole battery capacity and I gained a very interesting understanding into a couple beliefs that many on the left have about pricing and commerce that I think drives many of their negative views of corporations.

Tesla used to offer multiple battery sizes for different models but found demand for the lower range was small. They decided to standardize on the larger battery to save money in manufacturing and use software to offer a lower range model at a discount with the option to pay for the extra capacity later.

This has drawn ire as people are upset that higher range model could apparently be cheaper and that the lower range model is being artificially limited below its physical limits.

This tells me that there are a couple beliefs at play here. First, that the value of something has any relationship whatsoever to the cost to produce it (or of its inputs); essentially an objective value standard like Marx's labor theory of value. Second, that a purchase is anything more than an agreement; the belief the only valid sale is one where the buyer gains full rights to use the material purchased in any way physically possible.

While these views are entirely incorrect--a good's value is whatever a buyer is willing to pay and any voluntary agreement is perfectly valid--understanding that they underpin many progressives' complaints about business practices is very useful.
